Morning slipped into the kitchen like a shy cat, curling around the warm glow of the old stove. The coffee brewed, dark and stubborn, releasing a perfume that curled up the curtains and made the house feel awake. Outside, rain pattered against the windows in a steady rhythm, each drop a tiny drumbeat against the glass. I watched the world blur, the streetlights reflecting like copper coins on a pond, and thought about how time folds itself into ordinary moments.  

Memory, that fickle archivist, pulled me back to a summer in which the sky was an endless sapphire and cicadas sang in unison, their chorus a soundtrack to endless afternoons. A bicycle lay abandoned on a gravel path, its rusted chain a silent reminder that journeys sometimes halt, only to begin again later. I imagined the bicycle’s owner—perhaps a child with scraped knees, perhaps a weary traveler—pedaling toward an unknown horizon, each turn of the wheels a small rebellion against inertia.  

In the present, the kettle hissed, announcing the arrival of tea, and I lifted the cup, feeling the porcelain’s coolness seep into my palm. The steam rose, a ghostly veil, and I inhaled, letting the warmth spread through my chest. There, between the past and present, between rain and steam, I found a quiet gratitude for the fleeting symphonies of life, each note brief yet resonant, urging me to listen more closely. So I will keep writing, collecting these fleeting breaths, hoping they become lanterns that guide anyone wandering through ever dusk.
